finding: This round replaced the withdrawn sink-validation mechanism with a normative PRECONDITION on the release's own default, and then ships the default anyway, so §2 asserts both sides of the same gate. Line 88-93: 'before `blocking` may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author, and the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition. Four incompatible answers to the second exist and this section picks none of them ... which is why §7 has no test for it yet.' Line 111 then reads 'Default. `blocking`'. So the release ships as its default the exact behaviour it has just declared may not gate until two conditions it does not meet are met. Worse, §2 also asserts the FIRST condition is already satisfied: line 105-107 says `severity` 'is checkable against the finding's own text by a later round, which is what every round of this cycle has been doing to the round before it' -- present tense, no mechanism needed. Two engineers therefore write opposite tests and both cite §2: one asserts `blocking` is refused (or warns) until a checker exists, the other asserts nothing at all because the condition is met by construction. Neither can be falsified, because the 'four incompatible answers' are never enumerated -- a decomposer cannot pick one and a tester cannot name the observable that separates them.
suggestion: Pick one of three and say which: (a) the precondition is met by later-round review, in which case delete 'before blocking may gate' and keep only the §2.1 measurement as the argument; (b) the precondition is not met, in which case the default must be `all` in THIS release with `blocking` opt-in, and §7 gains a test that the shipped default is `all`; (c) the precondition is real and unmet and the field does not ship. Whichever is chosen, enumerate the four answers for the 67 rows with the one selected marked, or move that whole question to a named later release and drop it from this release's requirements -- an unenumerated 'four answers, none picked' is not a requirement a task can be written against.

finding: §2.0a's closing sentence (line 150-151) is the only place this release takes back the --check half, and it makes a false claim about its own document plus an untestable one about the code: 'It takes it back: `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`, and §7 gains the test that pins them equal.' §7 is byte-identical to round 1 -- eight tests, none of them about --check -- so 'gains' names a test that does not exist, and the clause that makes the release shippable (§2.0a line 145-150: without it, blocking 'changes nothing about the command an operator or `tp run` actually gates on') has no acceptance. The deeper defect is that the obvious form of the promised test passes against UNMODIFIED tp today and therefore cannot fail for the reason the clause exists: `--record` computes consecutive_clean at audit_record.go:101 and `--status`/`--check` at audit_record.go:339, and both are `engine.ConsecutiveClean(rounds)` over the SAME stored `Clean` booleans (stamped once at audit_record.go:71 as `findings == 0`). An equality assertion over those two payloads is green before a line of this release is written. And 'the same predicate' silently decides a fork §3 declares OPEN: §3 line 214-218 says 'Either audit's clean flag is recomputed live from rows ... or the disposition has to survive into the next round's input -- and this release has to pick one'. --check reading the same predicate as --record is only implementable under live recomputation, so §2.0a picks the fork §3 says is unpicked, in the same release, without saying so.
suggestion: State the mechanism, then state the test with the fixture that makes it discriminate. Mechanism: audit's --status must recompute each round's clean flag live from its recorded rows under the resolved audit_converge_on before calling ConsecutiveClean/Converged -- the shipped review twin does exactly this and is the citation §2.0a is missing (review_status.go:57-65 overwrites rounds[i].Clean with engine.ReviewRoundClean, and its comment gives the reason: it 'lets switching the setting or resolving a finding re-evaluate a round without re-recording'). Test: record round 1 and round 2 under audit_converge_on=all from a results file whose only non-PASS rows are severity `warning`, so both rounds store clean:false and --status --check exits 1; then `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` and, WITHOUT recording anything, assert (i) `tp audit spec.md --status` reports consecutive_clean 2 and converged true, (ii) `tp audit spec.md --status --check` exits 0, and (iii) those values equal what a `--record` re-run of the same file reports. Then flip back to `all` and assert all three revert. A stored-flag implementation fails (i)-(iii) and passes the trivial equality, which is what separates the two designs. Add the mirror case -- one `error` row -- so the test cannot pass by ignoring severity entirely.

finding: §7 as written cannot be green: two of its eight tests assert the exact negation of assertions inside ONE shipped guard test, and neither §6 nor §7 disposes of that guard, so a unit implementing §7 discovers the conflict only when the suite goes red and has no spec text telling it which side wins. internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503 TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate asserts: (a) lines 472-474, `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` exits non-zero with 'unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on' -- §7 test 1 requires the same literal to resolve through the documented precedence; (b) lines 480-487, after `tp audit results.ndjson --resolve go-safety:go-safety-item wontfix parked` the re-recorded round still reports go-safety consecutive_clean 0 / open 1, commented 'a wontfix disposition does not clear go-safety's open finding' -- §3 and §7 test 5 require a `wontfix` row to be excluded from the finding count; (c) line 489-490, `tp audit spec.md --status --check` still exits 1 'over the disposed finding' -- the same inversion on the gated surface. The test's own header (lines 454-468) is a written record of the Non-Goal it enforces and of the v0.35.0 amendment that already had to edit it once, so the retirement precedent exists and this spec does not use it. §6 Non-Goal 3 was updated this round to bind against the withdrawn validator, which shows the Non-Goal list was revisited and this guard still not addressed.
suggestion: Add a §7 test that names the guard's disposition explicitly, in the form v0.35.0 used on the same file: 'TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate's three Non-Goal-2/5 assertions are replaced by their inverses, and the surviving half -- that no OTHER escape hatch exists (a per-role threshold, a scope label, a streak entry with a fourth key) -- is kept verbatim.' Without that sentence the release has no answer to 'is the shipped assertion wrong, or is my implementation wrong', and the reviewer-facing effect is worse than a missing test: it is a test that says the release must not exist.

finding: The caveat paragraph added this round states a normative 'must not' that the release's own default provably does in both cycles it measures, hands the remedy to a different unshipped spec, and gives §7 nothing to assert. Lines 153-159: 'A severity gate is right, and it must not become a default stop at round 3 that ends rounds which would have changed their own method.' §2.1's table (line 166-169) says `blocking` converges at round 3 in BOTH cycles -- measured and confirmed here from the recorded rows: v0.35.0 r2/r3 and v0.36.0 r2/r3 each carry zero `error` rows, so with audit_clean_rounds:2 the stop is round 3 in both. And the rounds the caveat is about are v0.36.0's r12 and r13, which carry 2 `error` and 2 `error`+1 `warning` -- nine and ten rounds past the stop the shipped default would impose. So the release ships a default that violates its own 'must not' in 2 of 2 measured cases. The remedy named is `spec/0.49.0.md` §1c, which CLAUDE.md lists as pre-design and last of thirteen; until it ships the 'must not' is enforced by nothing. As a test: 'must not become a default stop at round 3 that ends rounds which would have changed their own method' has no observable -- there is no field, flag or exit code distinguishing a round that changed its method from one that re-read, so no assertion can be written and no implementation can be judged against it.
suggestion: Either demote it to a non-normative note ('an operator running blocking should expect to lose the late method-changing rounds; spec/0.49.0.md §1c is the intended answer'), or make it binding by making the default `all` until 0.49.0 §1c ships, or give it an observable this release can carry -- e.g. --record emits an advisory naming the rounds that would have been cut when the blocking stop is reached with non-blocking rows still open, and §7 asserts the advisory's presence and wording. A 'must not' with no mechanism, no test and its remedy in the thirteenth of thirteen planned releases is a sentence no reviewer or task can act on.

finding: §4 identifies, in this round's own text, the one way this release can silently break another phase -- and §7 contains no test that would catch it, so the broken implementation passes the whole list. §4 lines 243-246: '`engine.ConsecutiveClean` is shared with review's `--status` (`review_status.go:91`). Changing the walk changes both phases unless the reset is applied by the audit caller, and Non-Goal 4 says this release does not touch review.' Every one of tests 6, 7 and 8 is satisfied by the WRONG implementation: test 6 (--record resets on a differing spec_hash) passes if the walk itself was changed; test 7 (no recorded round is deleted or rewritten) passes because neither form writes; test 8 ('a cycle whose spec never changes records an identical streak') is audit-side and spec-unchanged, which is precisely the case where the two forms agree. So the release ships with Non-Goal 4 asserted in prose and guarded by nothing. §4 also never says what 'the audit-caller form' IS, and the shipped twin shows there is more than one shape it could take: review's --status does not change the walk either -- it overwrites rounds[i].Clean in memory before calling the shared ConsecutiveClean (review_status.go:63-67) -- so 'applied by the audit caller' covers at least a pre-filter of the slice, a wrapper function, and a second parameter, and §7 cannot tell them apart.
suggestion: Add a review-side regression test to §7 and pin the fixture, because the audit-side tests cannot see this: record three CLEAN review rounds whose spec_hash goes A, A, B (edit the spec between rounds 2 and 3), then assert `tp review spec.md --status` still reports consecutive_clean 3 and that its review_rounds[] entries are unchanged. Today that value is 3 (review_status.go:91 walks the flags with no hash boundary); the shared-walk implementation of §4 makes it 1, and this is the only assertion in the release that distinguishes them. Add the audit mirror -- rounds A, A, B all clean, audit consecutive_clean 1 -- so the pair pins the reset as audit-only rather than merely present.

finding: The §4 reset is pinned on `--record` only, and `--record` is not the surface anything gates on. Test 6 reads '`tp audit --record` with a `spec_hash` differing from the previous round resets `consecutive_clean` to zero and reports the reset on the machine-readable surface.' The command an operator, `tp run` and CI actually gate on is `tp audit <spec> --status --check` (audit_record.go:401-403 exits ExitValidation when !converged), and its consecutive_clean is computed on a different line by a different call (audit_record.go:339) from a different round slice than --record's (:101). Nothing in §7 asserts the reset appears there, so an implementation that resets on the --record payload alone -- entirely plausible, since §4's 'reports the reset' names no field and --record is the only command test 6 mentions -- ships green while the gate keeps reporting the pre-reset streak. This is the same split §2.0a line 150 promises to close for the predicate ('--check reads the same predicate as --record') and, like that one, §7 does not carry it. Two further observables are unpinned and both are needed for a deterministic assertion: 'reports the reset' names no key (is it a new boolean, a note, or just the changed consecutive_clean value?), and `stale` already goes true on the same input (engine.StateStale, audit_record.go:334), so a test author cannot tell whether the existing `stale` field IS the report or whether a new one is required.
suggestion: Rewrite test 6 as two assertions over both surfaces with a named key: 'After recording round 3 under a spec_hash differing from rounds 1-2, both `tp audit <spec> --record` and `tp audit <spec> --status` report consecutive_clean 0, and both carry <named key> identifying the reset; `--status --check` exits 1.' Then say in §4 whether the report is the pre-existing `stale` field or a new one, and if new, name it and its type -- otherwise two engineers ship two different payloads and both satisfy the sentence.

finding: Test 4 hard-codes two numbers against a corpus nothing in the repository pins, and its own defence of runnability answers a different objection than the one that applies. It reads 'Replayed against this repository's nine recorded v0.35.0 audit rounds, `blocking` converges at round 3 and `all` at round 9 ... The replay reads `status` and `severity` off recorded rows and needs no spec snapshot, which is why it is runnable where `spec/0.43.0.md` §6's corpus gates are not.' The snapshot point is correct and I verified the expectations hold today: spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 has 9 rounds; r2 and r3 carry zero `error` rows (r2 {info 7, warning 5}, r3 {info 3, warning 2}) so `blocking` stops at 3, and r8/r9 are the only fully-PASS rounds so `all` stops at 9. But the test's inputs are live, mutable, committed repository state, not a fixture: any later `tp audit spec/0.35.0.md --record`, any `--resolve` writing a disposition into those round files, and `spec/0.45.0.md` §3's `--reconcile` (which rewrites a round's stored hash) each move the numbers, and the test then fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the predicate under test. That is the failure mode CLAUDE.md's own rule warns about -- a claim bound to a named artifact cannot rot silently, but only if the artifact is pinned -- and it is the same class as the suite-state wrapper's reason for existing: a test whose subject is a spec still sitting in the repository.
suggestion: Copy the nine audit-round-N.ndjson files (and the round entries they need) into internal/cli/testdata as a checked-in replay fixture, and add a census guard beside the assertion -- 9 rounds, 42 non-PASS rows, 3 of them `error` and those in rounds 1 and 4 -- so a fixture that drifts fails as a fixture problem rather than as a predicate problem. State in test 4 that the fixture is a copy, not a read of spec/.tp-review/.

finding: §2's opening paragraph still ends 'it is the reason the sink validation above is a precondition rather than a nicety' (line 36) -- and the withdrawal this round performed turned that from a wrong direction into a reference to nothing. Round 2's version of this row was positional (the sink validation was BELOW, at §2's fifth paragraph, not above). The text is byte-identical this round but its referent is gone: lines 66-93 now record the sink validation as a draft that 'was withdrawn in the round after it was written', and §6 Non-Goal 3 (lines 279-283, also rewritten this round) makes it out of scope -- 'Any future proposal that makes `--record` refuse a row is a different release.' So §2's first paragraph asserts that a precondition of this release is a mechanism the same section withdraws and the Non-Goals forbid. This is not cosmetic for a decomposer: it is the sentence that tells a reader what the §2.1 measurement is FOR, and following it produces a task for a validator §6 explicitly bans. The pattern is worth naming because it is the second instance in this file this round -- a repair that removed a mechanism did not sweep the sentences that depended on it (the other is §2.0a's '§7 gains the test', filed separately).
suggestion: Repoint or delete it. If the intended referent is the requirement paragraph (lines 88-93), write 'it is the reason the checkability requirement below is a precondition rather than a nicety'; if the intent died with the withdrawn draft, end the paragraph at 'not 1 of 2. That is the honest case against the default.' Then sweep §2, §2.0a and §2.1 for every remaining sentence whose subject is the withdrawn validator -- a mechanism removed mid-round leaves references the same way a renumbered spec does, and CLAUDE.md already asks for that sweep after a move.

finding: NEAR-MISS (not a spec defect; recorded as asked). Reading §2.0a's new closing sentence -- 'It takes it back: `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`' -- my first conclusion was that this was a clean repair: the round-2 complaint was that the release opened a gap it did not close, and the release now closes it, so nothing to file. Two things refuted that before I wrote it off. First, §7 is byte-identical to round 1, so 'and §7 gains the test that pins them equal' is false about the document making the claim. Second, and the part I would have missed entirely: audit_record.go:101 (--record) and :339 (--status/--check) ALREADY call the same function, engine.ConsecutiveClean, over the same stored Clean flags -- so 'reads the same predicate' is true today, and the natural test of it passes against unmodified tp. The wrong conclusion would have been to accept a sentence that is simultaneously false about §7 and vacuous about the code. Shape worth naming: a repair phrased as 'X reads the same thing as Y' is unfalsifiable whenever X and Y already share a call, and it reads as a decision precisely because the reader assumes they did not.
suggestion: When a spec claims two surfaces now agree, check whether they already did -- if they did, the sentence is describing the defect rather than fixing it, and the fix is to name the input on which they must agree and today do not.

finding: NEAR-MISS (not a spec defect; recorded as asked). I drafted a finding that §7 test 7 ('The reset does not delete or rewrite any recorded round') is unfalsifiable, on §4's own words: 'zero stored bytes ... which makes §7 test 7 true by construction rather than by fixture' -- a test the spec advertises as unable to fail, against CLAUDE.md's rule that a test never observed failing proves nothing. It is wrong, and I caught it by asking what mutation kills it: test 7 fails under the alternative implementation §4 rejects, one that stores a reset counter or rewrites the round entries, so it discriminates between the two candidate designs and is exactly the guard that keeps the chosen one honest. 'True by construction' is a statement about the chosen implementation, not about the test's power. The wrong conclusion would have been to attack the one §7 test that IS a real design guard while the tests around it (6 and 8) are the ones that pass under both designs. Shape worth naming: 'this test cannot fail' is only a defect if no reachable implementation makes it fail -- the question is which implementations it discriminates, not whether it fails on the intended one.
suggestion: Before filing a vacuity finding on any test, name the mutation that would kill it; if one exists, the test is a guard and the finding belongs on its neighbours instead.

finding: RE-EXAMINATION of my own round-2 rows, recorded as asked; not a new defect. (1) My round-2 CRITICAL on §2.1's v0.36.0 row is RESOLVED and the reasoning was right. The cell now reads '13, never converged | round 3 (r2, r3 carry zero error) | never -- no round reaches zero', which is what I asked for and what the corpus says: re-measured this round from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0, all 13 rounds carry clean:false, r2 {warning 5, info 3} and r3 {warning 4, info 7} carry zero error, and every round including r13 {error 2, warning 1} holds at least one non-PASS row. The v0.35.0 row also survives re-measurement (r2/r3 zero error; r8/r9 the only fully-PASS rounds, so `all` at 9), and §1's '3 error, 22 warning, 17 info' recomputes exactly. I withdraw nothing. (2) My round-2 HIGH `analogy-contradicts-mechanism` -- the sentence requiring --record to reject a missing severity 'the way an unknown category is', when the shipped category sink returns early on the empty case -- is no longer live text, and the withdrawal SATISFIES the reasoning as far as it goes: the contradictory instruction is gone and §2 now records the refutation instead of patching around it, which is the right disposition for a mechanism refuted twice in two rounds. But it MOVES the problem rather than closing it, and I have filed the two places it moved to as this round's rows: the replacement is a precondition on `blocking` that the release neither meets nor decides while shipping `blocking` as its default (§2, critical), and §2's opening paragraph still calls the withdrawn mechanism a precondition (§2, medium). The narrower judgement I still hold unchanged is the one under both: an analogy to shipped code ('the way X already does') is not a specification, and nothing in the current text stops the next mechanism from being written the same way.
suggestion: No action for this row itself. Treat it as the audit trail for the two rows it points at, and as the answer to whether round 2's tester still holds its own prior reasoning: on §2.1, yes and it is now fixed; on §2, yes, and the withdrawal relocated the defect rather than removing it.
